paras: The threatened lynching of Mendoza and David Walsh took place on September 22, 1888, in Sonoma County, California, when residents near Santa Rosa seized two youths accused of burning barns and threatened to lynch them. One dispatch said the pair confessed after being hanged for a short time, but the marshal prevented a lynching, and both were later convicted of arson.

About daylight on September 22, an old barn belonging to A. Clark, halfway between Petaluma and Santa Rosa, was set on fire, and Henry Himebauch's barn and a straw stack of F. Cook nearby were also burned. The same morning two wagonloads of grain belonging to a Mr. Davis were damaged when the sacks were ripped open.

According to a Petaluma dispatch, two boys "about 16 years old" were suspected, and "the people of the neighborhood" followed them and arrested them near Santa Rosa, where they lived. The same dispatch said that "after hanging them a short time it is said they confessed their guilt," without naming who did the hanging. A separate dispatch from San Francisco named the prisoners as a "Spaniard" called Mendoza and a boy, David Walsh, and said Walsh admitted that Mendoza had burned one of the barns. In that account, the residents "turned out and threatened to lynch" the two but were prevented by the marshal.

No arrest of anyone in the crowd appears in the coverage. On November 14 a Santa Rosa court convicted J. Mendoza, described as a seventeen-year-old "Mexican boy," of arson, and Walsh, aged fourteen, "fared similarly." Five days later Judge Pressley sentenced Mendoza to two years at San Quentin and Walsh to two years in the Boys' and Girls' Reformatory Aid Institution at San Francisco, a sentence made light because of his youth.

The episode reached readers mainly through two Associated Press items, which the Los Angeles Herald printed on September 23 under the headline "Barns Wantonly Burned by Youthful Vandals" and the subhead "THREATENED LYNCHING." The Arizona Weekly Citizen ran the same dispatches a week later among other telegrams, spelling the boy's name "Welsh." Neither paper commented on the crowd's conduct, and the hanging was reported only as something "it is said" had happened.

The Sacramento Daily Record-Union mentioned only that Walsh, "an American boy," and "a Spaniard named Mendosa" were under arrest and had confessed, leaving out the hanging and the threat. Its later reports treated the pair as criminals, heading the conviction story "BAD BOYS" and noting that Mendoza had figured in criminal cases before.

The accounts differ on what the crowd did: the Petaluma dispatch reported a brief hanging, the San Francisco dispatch only a threat stopped by the marshal, and the Sacramento brief no violence at all. They also differ on ages, with the first dispatch calling both boys about sixteen and the November court report giving Mendoza's age as seventeen and Walsh's as fourteen.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Mendoza and David Walsh
bases: Residents pursued and seized two youths accused of barn burning, reportedly hanged them briefly until they confessed, and threatened to lynch them until the marshal intervened (A1, A3).

No one was killed: both accused were tried and sentenced months later (A4, A5); the brief hanging to force a confession and the threat to lynch were acts of a neighborhood crowd of unstated size, without lawful authority, over an arson accusation (A1, A3).

The arrests, confessions and later convictions are reported in several items (A1, A2, A4, A5), but the brief hanging and the lynching threat rest on two Associated Press dispatches carried together in A1 and A3, and the Sacramento brief mentions neither (A2).

accounts.label: Petaluma AP dispatch
accounts.gist: Two boys about 16 were suspected; the neighbors followed and arrested them near Santa Rosa, and 'it is said' they confessed after being hanged a short time.

accounts.label: San Francisco AP dispatch (advices from Santa Rosa)
accounts.gist: Names the arrested as Mendoza and David Walsh; Walsh admitted Mendoza burned a barn; residents threatened to lynch them but the marshal prevented it.

accounts.label: Sacramento brief
accounts.gist: Walsh and Mendosa under arrest for incendiarism and confessed; no hanging or mob mentioned.

accounts.label: Santa Rosa court reports
accounts.gist: Both convicted of arson in November and sentenced, Mendoza to San Quentin and Walsh to a reformatory.

framing.detail: The Los Angeles Herald ran the AP items under 'Barns Wantonly Burned by Youthful Vandals' and 'THREATENED LYNCHING', reporting the hanging as hearsay without comment on the crowd.
The Arizona Weekly Citizen ran the same dispatches without headline among other telegrams.
The Sacramento Record-Union reported only the arrest and confession, then the convictions under 'BAD BOYS' and 'Sonoma Criminals Sentenced'.
